lessons.title: Box<T>

answers: An enum can never refer to itself, boxed or not
The type would have infinite size without an indirection
An i32 payload is not allowed inside an enum
writing.exampleCaption: Without `Box`, this enum would need infinite size.
writing.explanation:
A recursive type has no fixed size, because each level would contain another whole level. `Box` has a known pointer size, so putting the recursive part behind one makes the type representable. `Box` also lets a function return a trait object whose concrete size is not known at the call site.

A recursive enum needs a known size at compile time. If `Tree::Node` directly contained two more `Tree` values, each of those nodes would contain more nodes with no finite size the compiler could lay out. `Box<Tree>` replaces each child with a pointer whose size is known. The actual child values live in separate heap allocations, and the boxes own them. Dropping the root recursively drops the owned children.

The sample's `sum` function borrows `&Tree`, matches on its variants, and reads through the boxes. It does not take ownership of the tree just to traverse it. Trace a root with two leaves and predict the sum before running the code. Then add one nested node and observe how the recursive call follows a box. This exercise shows the separation between the size of the enum variant and the depth of the runtime tree.

A box is also a way to own a value whose concrete type is hidden behind a trait object, `Box<dyn Trait>`. The box does not make every operation faster: following pointers and allocating each node can cost more than a compact flat representation. Use it when indirection expresses a real need, such as recursion or owned dynamic dispatch. For a simple fixed set of values, a `Vec<T>` or plain struct may be clearer. Choose the data shape first, then the pointer type that makes it representable.

The box is an owning pointer, so moving the box moves ownership of the child allocation without copying the entire tree. That makes recursive construction manageable while preserving deterministic cleanup.

writing.rule: `Box` gives a recursive or unsized value a known-size home.
writing.success: It compiles, and you can explain why `Box` is required.
writing.summary: `Box` moves a value to the heap behind a single owner.

A file is a source of bytes, not a ready-made collection of valid records. Give the parser a generic `R: BufRead` input so the same function can accept a buffered file, locked stdin, or an in-memory `Cursor`. This separates the data transformation from permissions, paths, and device-specific I/O. It also makes the parser easy to exercise without creating a real file.

The `lines()` iterator yields `io::Result<String>` values. First handle the read result, then decide what a line means. For this small report, trim whitespace, skip blank lines, and parse every other line as `i64`. A malformed nonblank line is an error, not a zero and not a reason to silently discard the record. Include the one-based physical line number in that error, even when earlier lines were blank.

Use `checked_add` when the accepted numeric domain can overflow the accumulator. Returning a clear error preserves the contract instead of making behavior depend on a debug or release overflow setting. Streaming avoids retaining every record, but one unusually long line can still allocate a large string. A production parser needs a separate record-size limit; buffering alone is not a memory quota.

lessons.title: Check, Build, Run

writing.exampleCaption: Three commands, three levels of evidence: types, an artifact, then a run.
writing.explanation:
`cargo check` proves type correctness without final code generation, build creates artifacts, and run executes a binary after building it. Fast feedback comes from asking only for the evidence you need.

The fastest useful command depends on the question you are asking. After an edit, `cargo check` verifies parsing, types, borrowing, and many other compiler rules without producing a final executable. `cargo test` compiles the test harness and runs tests. `cargo run` builds a binary if needed and executes it. `cargo build` produces an artifact without executing it. `cargo run` reuses what `cargo build` produced, while `cargo check` keeps its own output, and each command provides different evidence.

A productive loop is edit, check, test the changed behavior, then run the whole program when interaction matters. A successful `cargo check` does not prove a function returns the right answer; a passing unit test does not prove the CLI arguments are wired correctly. `cargo build --release` uses the release profile and is appropriate when validating a shippable artifact or measuring optimized performance. It is usually slower than a quick debug check during a small edit.

Try introducing a type mismatch and observe which command catches it first. Fix that, then introduce a logic bug that compiles but fails an assertion. Finally run the application with a representative input. Record what each stage established and what it left untested. This distinction prevents “it compiled” from becoming an overconfident claim. Keep the loop short while developing, and use broader checks at meaningful checkpoints rather than waiting until the end of the project.

For a library-only package, `cargo run` has no default binary to execute; choose an example or add a binary target. In a workspace, a command may need `-p package_name` to identify which member you mean. These small command choices keep feedback focused.

writing.question: Which command skips final code generation?
writing.rule: `cargo check` proves type correctness without final code generation, build creates artifacts, and run executes a binary after building it.
writing.success: You can name the fact each command proved and the fact it left untested.
writing.summary: Choose the cheapest command that proves the next fact.

lessons.title: Reference Cycles

answers: A Weak link is cheaper to clone than an Rc
Two Rc links in a cycle never reach zero, so nothing is freed
The compiler refuses to build a cyclic Rc graph
writing.exampleCaption: The child points back with `Weak`, so the cycle never forms.
writing.explanation:
Two `Rc` handles pointing at each other never reach a count of zero, so neither is freed. `Weak<T>` is the answer: it does not count towards ownership and must be upgraded before use, which turns a parent pointer into something that can legitimately be gone.

Reference counting releases an allocation only when its strong count reaches zero. If node A owns an `Rc` to B and B owns an `Rc` back to A, each keeps the other alive after all outside handles are dropped. Rust prevents memory unsafety here, but the allocations leak. A graph needs a deliberate ownership direction, not strong links in every direction.

A common tree design lets a parent own children through strong `Rc` handles while each child keeps a `Weak` reference back to its parent. A weak reference does not keep the parent alive. `upgrade()` returns an `Option<Rc<T>>`, because the parent may have been dropped. That absence is a normal state to handle, not an exceptional failure. In the sample, `Rc::downgrade` stores the parent link, and the `Option` from `upgrade()` is checked before reading through it.

Draw two nodes and label the strong links before writing code. Remove all external owners on paper: if every node still has an incoming strong link from within the cycle, cleanup cannot begin. Replace one direction with weak links and repeat the count. For practice, create a parent and child, then drop the parent and verify that upgrading the child's weak parent link returns `None` if the child is still held externally. The lesson is not to avoid shared ownership entirely, but to make the owning direction explicit.

Weak references can also be used for caches that should not keep objects alive. The caller must accept that `upgrade()` may return `None`; a weak link is a question about whether the target still exists, not an ownership guarantee. Draw strong and weak edges with different arrows during review.
writing.feedback: Ownership should flow one way; the back-reference observes without owning.
writing.question: Why should that parent link be Weak?
writing.rule: `Weak` does not keep a value alive, so `upgrade()` may return `None`.
writing.success: You can name which direction owns and which merely observes.
writing.summary: Rust prevents data races, not leaks — a cycle can still strand memory.
writing.task: Explain where a parent pointer should be Weak rather than `Rc`.

lessons.title: Dependencies

writing.exampleCaption: A requirement, a feature set, and an opt-out of defaults.
writing.exampleCode:
[dependencies]
serde = "=1.0.229"
serde_json = "=1.0.151"
smallvec = "1"
memchr = { version = "2", default-features = false }
writing.explanation:
"1.2" means any 1.x at or above 1.2, because Cargo follows SemVer: patch and minor releases must stay compatible. The resolver picks the highest match and records the exact choice in `Cargo.lock`, and features let one crate ship optional pieces you opt into rather than paying for by default.

A dependency declaration is a compatibility request, not a permanent pin. In Cargo's default caret requirement, `version = "1.2"` accepts compatible 1.x releases from 1.2 upward but not 2.0. `Cargo.lock` records the concrete versions selected for a particular resolution, so two developers can rebuild the same application graph. Read both files when investigating why a new release did or did not appear in your build.

Features let a dependency expose optional capabilities. In the example, `serde` with `derive` enables procedural derives; `default-features = false` on another dependency removes only that dependency edge's default request. Features are unified when the same package is reached through several paths, so another dependency can still turn a feature on. Treat features as additive options, and inspect the resolved feature graph when behavior surprises you.

Before adding a crate, check what problem it solves, whether its API fits the project, and what it brings into the build. A small dependency can be worthwhile, but every dependency adds a maintenance and security surface. Pinning every version forever is not a substitute for tests; compatible updates still need verification. Practice with `cargo tree` to inspect the graph, update one package deliberately, and run tests after the lockfile changes. Keep direct dependency declarations clear and leave transitive selection to the resolver unless a real constraint requires intervention.

When reading a version requirement, pay attention to pre-release versions and major version zero, whose compatibility rules are narrower. Do not infer safety solely from a SemVer range; examine release notes and run meaningful tests after updates.

lessons.title: Dependency Kinds

writing.exampleCaption: `log` is part of the normal graph; `pretty_assertions` is available only to tests, examples, and benchmarks.
writing.exampleCode:
[dependencies]
log = "0.4"

[dev-dependencies]
pretty_assertions = "1"
writing.explanation:
Normal dependencies become part of a target graph, build dependencies support build scripts, and dev dependencies exist for tests and examples. The distinction keeps production graphs smaller and clearer.

Cargo separates dependencies by the role they play in a package. Normal `[dependencies]` are needed to build the library or binary target. `[build-dependencies]` are available to a `build.rs` script that runs during the build, often to generate files or detect native libraries. `[dev-dependencies]` support tests, examples, and benchmarks but are not ordinary runtime dependencies of the published library. The distinction helps make a package's requirements understandable.

Read the sample manifest and ask where each crate is used. A logging interface needed by production code belongs under normal dependencies. A prettier assertion formatter used only in tests belongs under dev dependencies. Moving it into normal dependencies may unnecessarily expand consumers' build graphs. Conversely, placing a production import under dev dependencies makes a normal build fail even if tests happen to compile in a different configuration.

Dependency kinds do not by themselves make a crate trustworthy or small. Versions, features, and transitive dependencies still matter. Use `cargo tree` with the relevant target or feature flags to inspect the resolved graph. Add one test-only helper and confirm `cargo build` does not need its API in production code. Then add a build script only if there is a real build-time task; generated code adds another layer to debug. Treat each manifest section as a statement of when that capability is actually required.

lessons.title: Deref & Drop

answers: Only when you call drop() on it explicitly
Automatically when the value leaves scope
At program exit, once main has returned
writing.exampleCaption: Deref coercion is why `&MyBox<String>` reaches a `&str` parameter.
writing.explanation:
Implementing Deref lets the compiler insert conversions automatically, which is why `&String` works where `&str` is expected. Drop lets a type run code when it goes out of scope, and the two together are how smart pointers feel built in — a `Box` behaves like the value it holds and cleans up on its own.

`Deref` tells Rust how a pointer-like wrapper exposes a reference to its target. In the example, `MyBox<T>` can return `&T` from its inner field, so code can read the wrapped value through familiar syntax. Deref coercion can adapt `&String` to `&str` through the type's implementations. This convenience should be predictable: implementing `Deref` for a type that is not really pointer-like can make method resolution and ownership harder to understand.

`Drop` describes cleanup when an owner leaves scope. A wrapper around a file or other resource can release it in `drop`, and the caller does not need to remember an explicit cleanup line on every path. You cannot normally call a value's `drop` method directly; `std::mem::drop(value)` consumes it and triggers cleanup early. A moved wrapper is dropped by its new owner, not again at the old binding.

Build a small wrapper, implement `Deref`, and call a method from the inner type through it. Then add a `Drop` implementation that logs when cleanup happens. Place one wrapper in an inner block and predict the log order. Keep the wrapper's behavior unsurprising: `Deref` for transparent access, `Drop` for resource cleanup. If the wrapper needs complex policy or fallible access, explicit methods often communicate more clearly than pretending it is the target value.

Remember that `Drop::drop` receives `&mut self`, so it can inspect and release fields but cannot move arbitrary fields out as if the object were still complete. The compiler still drops fields after the method returns. Avoid panicking in destructors, especially during unwinding, and keep cleanup as reliable as possible.

Test the exact point where each wrapper leaves scope.
writing.feedback: Drop runs at the end of the value's scope; `std::mem::drop` just ends it sooner.
writing.question: When does that Drop message print?
writing.rule: Deref coercion applies repeatedly until the types line up.
writing.success: The call compiles without an explicit conversion.
writing.summary: Deref makes your type usable like a reference to another one.

lessons.title: Executable Documentation

writing.exampleCaption: The `assert_eq!` in the doc comment is compiled and run by `cargo test`.
writing.explanation:
Rust documentation examples in Rust code fences can compile and run as tests during `cargo test`, unless their fence attributes opt out or change execution. A small realistic example teaches usage and fails when an API change makes the documentation stale.

A documentation example is a small public usage test. A Rust code block in a `///` comment can be compiled and run by rustdoc during `cargo test`. The sample demonstrates `add_one` with an assertion, so a changed return value can fail the documentation check. In a library crate named `demo`, the example imports the public item as `demo::add_one`; use the actual crate name in a real package. Documentation that calls an item without bringing it into scope can fail even when the function itself is correct.

Keep a doc example focused on the call a user is likely to make, including setup only when needed. Explain the purpose, important input constraints, and meaning of the return value in prose. You can hide incidental setup lines with rustdoc's `#` marker, but the behavior being promised should remain visible. Some fences are marked `no_run` or `ignore` for specific reasons; those attributes affect whether a block executes, so avoid claiming every fenced block is automatically a test.

Run `cargo test --doc` after changing a public API and see whether the example still works. Try deliberately changing the asserted value to observe the failure. Then add an edge-case example if it clarifies behavior, but resist turning documentation into a long test suite. A good example is both readable on the docs page and executable in the test harness. It prevents a common drift: code changes while the published instructions continue teaching an obsolete call.

If a code block requires network access or another external resource, it may be unsuitable as a routine doctest. Show the API in a short self-contained example and put slower environment-dependent checks in integration tests. Keep the documentation honest about what runs automatically.

writing.explanation:
A useful error says what operation failed and retains the original cause. Add context at abstraction boundaries rather than replacing specific information with one vague message.

An error should carry enough information for someone at the boundary to understand what failed. `text.parse::<u16>()` can report a parsing failure, but a caller may need to know that this text was supposed to be a port. The example's `map_err` adds the offending value and the operation while preserving the underlying cause in the formatted message. At a higher layer, you might add which configuration file or command supplied that value.

The useful question is where to add context. A low-level parser knows syntax; a configuration loader knows the field name; a CLI knows what the user was trying to do. Each layer should add only the information it owns. Replacing every error with the same "invalid input" string erases evidence. Duplicating full messages at every layer produces noise. Structured error types or source chains can preserve machine-readable causes until the final presentation layer chooses wording.

Try the port function with valid text, letters, and a number too large for `u16`. Check that the user-facing message distinguishes where the failure occurred without exposing irrelevant internal details. If recovery is possible, return `Result` so the caller can decide. If the error is logged, include enough context to reproduce it while avoiding secrets or full sensitive input. Good diagnostics are a collaboration between error type, call-site context, and final display—not a single catch-all message.

writing.summary: Optional capability must preserve the old consumer across the supported feature sets.
writing.rule: Keep the baseline API working with defaults, minimal builds and supported feature unions.
writing.explanation:
A feature is part of a package's public contract when downstream users can request it. This example preserves `label(7) == "core=7"` while adding `details` and `trace` functions. The existing consumer does not change when either feature is enabled. The two features can be requested together, and the base `label` keeps the same signature and behavior. That is the observable promise the matrix checks.

Cargo combines feature requests for a package within the applicable resolution context. One dependency path can request `details` and another can request `trace`, so code that only compiles with exactly one of them is a downstream hazard. Newer resolver versions isolate some contexts, such as certain build or development dependencies; this does not turn ordinary feature requests into global exclusion switches. Keep the example's two functions differently named and additive. A broken alternative that defines the same helper name under both features may pass each individual build and fail their union.

Check a small, explicit matrix rather than trusting `--all-features` alone. Include defaults, `--no-default-features`, each optional feature, and supported combinations. The all-features build can accidentally hide a missing item in the minimal profile. Conversely, checking each feature alone misses collisions when consumers request both. For a large feature set, select combinations from the documented contract and known interactions; checking a few combinations is not a claim to have exhausted an exponential space.

Use a downstream consumer of the library target, not only tests that live inside its private module tree. Keep that consumer's source bytes fixed while changing the requested dependency features. Assert both the baseline rendering and each requested optional API. The accompanying fixture compiles and runs this consumer on the minimum and current compilers. It also checks a candidate that changes baseline rendering only when `details` is enabled, and one whose duplicate helper exists only in the union. Each should fail for a different reason.

`default-features = false` is an edge request to avoid enabling that dependency's defaults; it is not a command to disable defaults that another dependency path requests. The fixture includes two paths to demonstrate this distinction. Be cautious when removing an existing default feature, renaming an optional capability, changing its implied dependencies or increasing the compiler requirement of that feature. Review those changes under the same published compatibility policy as ordinary public methods.

lessons.title: Feature Design

writing.exampleCaption: Each build compiles exactly one `paint`, chosen by whether `color` is on.
writing.explanation:
Cargo features are unified across a dependency graph, so disabling one consumer's feature may not disable it globally. Prefer additive capabilities and avoid features that make the same API mean incompatible things.

A feature is a named, additive capability a crate can enable at compile time. `#[cfg(feature = "color")]` includes code only when that feature is active; another branch can provide behavior without it. A feature is not a runtime switch, so a binary cannot toggle it after compilation. The public API exposed under different feature sets should be understandable and tested in each supported configuration.

Cargo unifies feature requests for the same package in a dependency graph. If one dependency path asks for feature A and another asks for feature B, the package may be built with both. That makes mutually exclusive features fragile: downstream users can accidentally activate the combination. Prefer features that add independent capabilities and keep a sensible default. If two backends truly cannot coexist, document and enforce that constraint explicitly, or consider a different design.

Create a tiny crate with a `color` feature and compile it with and without `--features color`. Then add two dependents that request different features of the same library and inspect the resulting feature graph with `cargo tree -e features`. Test `--no-default-features` if you claim that mode works. Avoid assuming that setting `default-features = false` at one edge globally disables defaults; another path can enable them. Feature design is part of the compatibility contract, not only a way to reduce compile time.

A feature name should describe the capability it adds. Avoid names that merely encode an internal implementation file, because external users will depend on the public meaning over time.

A parser that never panics can still be wrong if it silently ignores a suffix, rounds an overflowing value, or accepts a missing field. Write down the accepted grammar before writing adversarial cases. This lesson's grammar is exactly two trimmed unsigned decimal byte values separated by one colon. Both values must fit u8. A third field, an empty field, a sign, or nondecimal text is invalid.

Organize tests by failure class instead of adding random strings without a hypothesis. Test a missing delimiter, repeated delimiters, a negative value, a leading plus, overflow, whitespace-only fields, Unicode digits, and the two valid numeric boundaries. Rust's numeric parser may accept syntax you did not intend, so enforce the grammar's ASCII-digit rule before parsing. Return None for this small API; a richer user-facing parser should expose a precise error type.

Avoid `filter_map` on fallible fields: it can turn a three-field record with one bad field into two apparently good values. Do not index a collected vector until its length has been checked. Check complete consumption so a valid prefix cannot conceal trailing junk. These ideas transfer directly to command input, imported project metadata, and network messages.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. The lab uses deterministic hostile cases. Desktop cargo-fuzz is a separate toolchain that can explore byte inputs and save crashes; it does not belong to the browser or iOS run profile merely because the parser itself is portable. A useful fuzz target asserts domain properties after successful parsing and never treats rejection of arbitrary bytes as a bug.

Files under `tests/` compile as separate crates and can only use the library's public API. That boundary catches accidental reliance on private implementation details.

An integration test behaves like an external user of your library. Each file under `tests/` is compiled as a separate crate and imports the public API by crate name. It cannot reach private helpers simply because they exist in the same repository. That constraint is valuable: if a test can accomplish a real task through the public interface, downstream callers probably can too.

A test that relies on shared mutable files or network state can fail intermittently and hide real regressions. Run `cargo test --test public_api` while developing that file, then `cargo test` for the full suite. When a test fails, distinguish a library behavior change from a test assumption that was never part of the public contract. `Cargo.toml` says which versions are acceptable; `Cargo.lock` records which exact package versions the resolver selected. If a manifest permits several compatible releases, the lockfile keeps subsequent ordinary builds on the same chosen graph until an update changes it. This helps a team reproduce a bug and compare results without silently pulling a newer dependency on every checkout.

An application normally commits its lockfile. A library crate may also commit one for its own development and tests, but downstream consumers resolve dependencies using their own lockfiles. If you are publishing a binary or deploying a service, review lockfile changes along with source changes, because a dependency update can alter behavior even when your own code is unchanged.

lessons.title: MSRV Is a Tested Promise
lessons.concept: A manifest declaration needs evidence from the minimum supported compiler

writing.summary: A manifest declaration needs evidence from the minimum supported compiler.
writing.rule: Test the actual minimum compiler and supported profiles; metadata alone is not evidence.
writing.explanation:
The minimum supported Rust version, or MSRV, is a support promise about the compiler and Cargo environment your package accepts. A `rust-version = "1.78"` declaration tells Cargo the stated minimum; it does not translate newer syntax or standard-library APIs into older equivalents. A current compiler can compile code that the minimum cannot. A release needs a minimum-version job as well as the ordinary current-version job.

Use a concrete failure. `Option::is_none_or` was stabilized in Rust 1.82. An implementation using that method can pass on a newer compiler while failing on 1.78, even if the manifest still says 1.78. The reading's `match` expresses the same optional-limit rule without that method: no configured value is permitted, zero is rejected, and a positive value must not exceed the ceiling. Check the boundary where the value equals the ceiling, and the case where the ceiling itself is zero.

A useful support record includes the declared compiler, edition, feature sets, targets, dependency resolution and tests performed. This unit's small fixtures use edition 2021 and a dependency-free lockfile understood by both tested toolchains. That keeps a standard-library API failure separate from an unrelated manifest or lockfile-format failure. In a real package, newer Cargo syntax, edition support, build scripts and procedural macros may raise the effective requirement before your own library source is compiled.

Run the actual supported toolchain, for example `cargo +1.78 check --locked` and `cargo +1.78 test --locked`, in an environment that has it installed. lessons.concept: Path, PathBuf, and lexical validation

writing.summary: Treat a path as structured input and keep lexical checks distinct from filesystem authority.
writing.rule: Joining a path is not permission checking, and lexical validation does not resolve symlinks.
writing.explanation:
Use `Path` for a borrowed path and `PathBuf` for an owned path that can be extended. Concatenating strings can mishandle separators and makes it difficult to see which input controls the destination. `root.join(name)` expresses the relationship, but it does not guarantee that the result stays beneath root. In particular, an absolute name can replace the beginning, and parent components can walk upward.

For the lab, accept only a nonempty sequence of normal relative components. Reject an absolute path, any parent component, and a path containing only current-directory components. Joining the accepted components gives a useful lexical rule for an imported project name. Spaces and Unicode are legitimate filename content; do not reject them merely because a shell command would need quoting. No shell command is involved in this operation.

This is deliberately not a complete security boundary for a hostile filesystem. A symlink inside root may point elsewhere, and checking a canonical path before opening it can race with a later replacement. Real authority comes from the host's granted directory handles and platform-specific safe open operations. A WebAssembly guest should not gain access to a user's home directory just because a path string looks harmless.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. The exercise manipulates paths without touching disk. The following file lesson demonstrates a granted sandbox destination. Keep these layers separate: parse a requested relative path, apply the host's access policy, and handle the actual open result. This separation is useful when importing archives or moving project files as well as when writing a command-line report.

writing.summary: A normalization function should satisfy laws on many inputs, not only one expected output.
writing.rule: Use an independent oracle; repeating the implementation in the assertion repeats its bugs.

A few examples help explain a function, while properties describe behavior across a family of inputs. For a canonical set of integer IDs, the output must be sorted, contain no duplicates, preserve membership, and be idempotent. None of those laws alone is enough: a function returning an empty vector is sorted and idempotent but discards every ID.

Compare against an independent model such as BTreeSet rather than copying the same sort-and-deduplicate sequence into the test. Generate bounded combinations from a small domain, including negative values and repeated IDs. Small exhaustive spaces are often excellent at finding boundary mistakes, are deterministic, and require no external dependency. They still establish evidence only for the inputs tested, not a proof for every vector length.

The compiler lab's private harness checks concrete outputs and generated membership behavior. A learner cannot make it pass merely by editing an assertion in the starter. The code under test remains editable; the verdict is produced by a separate harness after calls finish. Treat this as feedback about the exercise contract, not a hostile-code containment guarantee: arbitrary source remains inside the ordinary bounded local runtime.

lessons.concept: Compile the unchanged consumer before calling an API change compatible

writing.summary: Compile the unchanged consumer before calling an API change compatible.
writing.rule: Keep the original caller's signatures and promised behavior across supported releases.
writing.explanation:
A library release is used by code you do not own. Start the review with one unchanged downstream consumer: the original call to `Policy::new(3).unwrap().attempts()` must still compile and return three. A green library test suite is useful but can miss a break if those tests were edited together with the API. Compile the same consumer against both library versions instead of fixing it until it passes.

In the example, `attempts` and `delay_ms` are private. Callers construct `Policy` through `new`, so adding the private delay field does not require them to update a struct literal. The existing constructor keeps its parameter, return type and zero-attempt validation. `with_delay` is a new builder that retains the attempt count; omitting it still selects zero delay. This is a deliberately small compatible evolution of this consumer contract, not a proof that every private representation change is harmless.

An entirely public struct is a different contract. Adding a required field breaks a downstream literal that listed all the previous fields. Adding an enum variant can break an exhaustive downstream match. A `#[non_exhaustive]` design can reserve evolution space when chosen before callers depend on exhaustive construction or matching; adding that restriction later may itself break callers. For a public trait, remember that consumers may implement it as well as call it: a new required method affects those implementations.

Source compatibility is one part of the review. Changing an error condition, normalization rule, panic behavior or ordering can break an application that still compiles. Generic bounds, auto traits such as `Send`, lifetimes and documented layout or FFI promises can also matter. The private-field builder does not grant permission to change these properties silently. Write the behavior you promise, then choose a versioning and migration policy that matches it. Cargo's SemVer guidance describes conventions and caveats; a version number does not establish that an arbitrary change is safe.

Keep a downstream fixture outside the library's own module tests. Pin the consumer source bytes, compile it with the candidate library, run its observable assertions, and retain a deliberately incompatible candidate that the fixture rejects. A changed constructor arity should fail compilation; a constructor that quietly changes the attempt count should compile but fail the consumer assertion. These two failures demonstrate different checks. A finite fixture covers its consumers and inputs, not every possible external program.

Local compiler lab: implement the constructor, getters and builder in `solution.rs` without changing their public signatures. The separate harness calls the API with normal and boundary values and checks that the builder preserves the original attempt count. It does not accept an edited assertion or a printed success string as the implementation. The standard-library example and lab need no server or external crate. Full release CI should additionally test the supported targets, feature sets and compiler versions.

lessons.title: Rc & RefCell

writing.exampleCaption: Shared ownership on the outside, controlled mutation on the inside.
writing.explanation:
`Rc<T>` keeps a count and frees when it reaches zero, but only hands out shared references. Pairing it with `RefCell<T>` lets you mutate through that shared handle, with the borrow rules checked at runtime instead — a violation panics rather than failing to compile. Neither is thread-safe; that is `Arc` and `Mutex`.

`Rc<T>` provides shared ownership within one thread. Each clone of an `Rc` is another strong handle to the same allocation, not a deep copy of `T`. The allocation is released when its last strong owner disappears. Because multiple owners can access the same value, `Rc<T>` normally provides shared read access. Wrapping the value in `RefCell<T>` permits mutation by checking the borrow rule at runtime.

In the sample, both `shared` and `second` refer to the same cell. A `borrow_mut()` guard grants exclusive access while it is alive; a `borrow()` guard permits reading, possibly alongside other readers. If a writer and reader overlap, `RefCell` panics, or `try_borrow` returns an error. Keep the guard's lifetime short. If the mutation is awkward only because the ownership design is unclear, a simpler owner with explicit mutable borrowing may be preferable.

Use `Rc<RefCell<T>>` for a local graph or UI state where several single-threaded owners truly need to share a mutable value. It is not a concurrency primitive. `Rc` does not implement the thread-safety traits needed for cross-thread sharing, and `RefCell` does not synchronize threads. The rough cross-thread counterparts are `Arc<T>` for shared ownership and a `Mutex<T>` or another synchronization strategy for mutation. Draw each owner and each active borrow separately; counting handles and checking access are two different mechanisms.

If you need only several read-only owners, `Rc<T>` alone is simpler. Add `RefCell` only when mutation behind shared ownership is a real requirement.

opt-level = 3
lto = "thin"
debug = 1

Cargo profiles configure optimization, debug information, panic strategy, and more. Measure the real workload before trading compile time, binary size, or debuggability for speed.

A Cargo profile controls how a target is compiled. The default development profile favors fast builds and useful diagnostics; the release profile typically enables stronger optimization. Settings such as `opt-level`, `lto`, debug information, and panic behavior change compile time, runtime speed, binary size, or the quality of stack traces. There is no one best combination for every workload.

The sample enables optimization and thin link-time optimization while retaining some debug information. That is a reasonable candidate to measure, not a universal prescription. Compare debug and release builds on a representative task. If a binary is latency-sensitive, measure latency; if it must fit a size limit, measure bytes; if production crashes need investigation, keep enough symbols to diagnose them. A microbenchmark on an empty loop may say little about a real application doing I/O and allocation.

Use `cargo build --release` to create the optimized artifact, and keep tests running in the configurations you support. Some bugs only appear under different optimization or feature combinations, even though safe Rust prevents many memory errors. Record the baseline before changing a profile, change one setting, and compare the same workload. If the result is within noise, prefer the simpler configuration. Release settings should be driven by evidence and operational needs, not by copying every available optimization flag into the manifest.

writing.summary: Turn JSON into a transport type, validate it, and only then create a domain value.
writing.rule: Deserialization checks the transport shape; your domain invariants still need an explicit boundary.

JSON describes data exchange, while your application model describes valid state. Deserialize into a small transport structure, then convert it into a domain value whose constructor enforces the rules. A syntactically valid JSON object can still contain a blank display name, a negative quantity, or a count larger than the application supports. Do not spread those checks across every consumer.

Choose an evolution policy. Serde derive normally ignores unknown fields unless configured with `deny_unknown_fields`. This explicit visitor rejects unknown and duplicate fields itself. Neither choice is universally safer: rejecting surprises is useful for a tightly controlled command, while forward-compatible clients may need to tolerate new fields. Document the decision, and use an explicit format version when a later change would reinterpret an existing field.

Compare decoded meaning in a round-trip test rather than relying on object-key order or pretty-print whitespace. Avoid printing full input documents into error logs when they may contain private data. Limit input size before decoding untrusted text, and distinguish a parse error from a domain validation error. The lab in the previous lesson stays dependency-free; this lesson shows how to replace its intentionally restricted transport format with an established serialization library.

The visitor checks duplicate, missing and unknown fields while Serde checks each field type. A u32 rejects negative and overflowing counts. The separate decode function bounds input size and rejects blank names. Main asserts all of those failures as well as a Unicode round-trip; a successful JSON parse alone is not evidence of domain validity.

writing.exampleCaption: Tests live beside the code and can see its private parts.
writing.explanation:
`#[test]` registers functions with the test harness. A `#[cfg(test)]` module is excluded from ordinary builds, including `cargo build --release`, but included by `cargo test --release`. Test mode and optimization profile are separate choices. Unit tests sit beside the code and can reach its private details; integration tests live in `tests/` and see only the public API, which is a useful check on your own interface.

A test records an observable promise. `#[test]` marks a function that the test harness runs under `cargo test`; an assertion compares the actual value with a prediction. The sample puts tests beside the implementation in a `#[cfg(test)]` module, which is a good place for small unit tests of edge cases and private helpers. The module is only compiled when testing, so it does not become a normal production code path.

Start with a function that adds two numbers. Test a typical case, zero, and a boundary that might reveal overflow or an incorrect sign. Name tests for the behavior they protect rather than the implementation line they execute. If a test fails, its assertion should tell you what input produced the mismatch. A test that merely repeats the function's code is weak: it can share the same mistake. Prefer a simple expected result you can justify independently.

Integration tests under `tests/` compile as separate crates and call the public library API. They are useful when you want evidence that an external consumer can use the package as intended. A practical suite usually combines focused unit tests with a few end-to-end cases. Tests do not prove an implementation correct for every input, but they make intended behavior executable and guard against later changes. Run the narrowest relevant test while editing and the full suite before shipping; both speeds of feedback matter.

Compare `cargo test` and `cargo test --release`: both execute assertions. Integer overflow checks normally differ between the default dev and release profiles, and projects can override that policy. Write explicit checked arithmetic when overflow is part of the API contract, rather than relying on the test profile.

lessons.title: Keep a Unicode Regression
lessons.concept: A minimal failure that survives a refactor

writing.summary: Turn a real boundary failure into a small, named case that protects future changes.
writing.rule: Define the unit before testing a text limit: bytes, scalar values, and grapheme clusters differ.
writing.explanation:
Suppose a preview function once sliced text at a byte offset and panicked on an accented character. Replacing it with a character iterator fixes that specific bug, but keep a regression that would fail under the old implementation. A test named after the behavior, such as truncates_at_scalar_boundary, is more useful than one named after an unrelated ticket number.

The contract here is to keep at most n Unicode scalar values and add no ellipsis. Return all text when it is shorter than n, and an empty string when n is zero. This is not a display-column limit or a grapheme-cluster limit. An e followed by a combining accent consists of two scalar values; stopping after one may produce a visually surprising but contractually valid result. A user-interface preview may need a grapheme-aware library instead.

A strong regression set contains the smallest original failure, zero, an empty input, an oversized limit, and a neighboring ASCII case. Add a property that the result is a prefix at a valid UTF-8 boundary and contains at most the requested number of scalar values. Avoid assuming that String::len counts characters; it counts bytes.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. The lab compiles the changed function and checks the regression cases independently. Before changing the contract to add an ellipsis, decide whether the ellipsis counts toward the limit and whether existing callers depend on exact output. Good tests document that contract; they should not freeze every internal implementation choice or discourage a clearer iterator-based solution.

writing.summary: Specify a small input format before implementing its parser.
writing.rule: Malformed records must not disappear from a successful report.
writing.explanation:
The report format in this exercise is intentionally smaller than CSV: one nonblank record per line, exactly two comma-separated fields, a nonempty trimmed name, and an unsigned count. Quoting and escaped commas are unsupported and must be rejected. Calling a split-on-comma parser a complete CSV parser would be misleading; real CSV permits quoted delimiters, embedded newlines, and escaped quote characters.

Parse the entire record before changing the report total. Validate the number of fields, trim both fields, check that the name is nonempty, and parse the count as `u32`. Report a typed or clearly documented error instead of substituting zero. At an application boundary, attach a one-based line number while preserving enough information to explain whether the structure or the number was invalid.

The compiler lab focuses on one record so its contract stays small. A later adapter can reuse the buffered-line reader, skip blank lines, and call this parser. A successful parse returns owned data that can outlive the input buffer. If ownership costs become significant, consider a borrowed intermediate representation, but measure before introducing lifetimes into every public API.

Local compiler profile: standard library only. Tests cover whitespace, zero, extra fields, missing fields, a negative count, overflow, and unsupported quotes. These cases are examples of a broader rule: input validation is a part of the data model, not a cosmetic step at the end. Before extending this format, decide whether an established CSV crate is a better fit than adding another exception to a home-grown grammar.

answers: One lockfile and one target directory
writing.exampleCaption: One root manifest, many members, one shared lockfile.
writing.exampleCode:
# Cargo.toml at the workspace root
[workspace]
resolver = "3"
members = ["core", "cli"]

# cli/Cargo.toml
[dependencies]
core = { path = "../core" }
writing.explanation:
Members share a target directory and lockfile, while the resolver may still select multiple versions of a dependency when requirements are incompatible. Splitting a project into a library plus a thin binary is the usual first move, because it makes the library testable on its own.

A Cargo workspace groups packages that are developed together. A root `Cargo.toml` lists members such as `core` and `cli`; the packages share a lockfile and build output directory, and workspace commands can operate across members. A common design puts reusable behavior in a library and keeps the binary thin: the CLI parses arguments, calls library functions, and prints a result. This makes the core easier to test and reuse.

The example's dependency path from `cli` to `core` is explicit in the CLI manifest. Being in the same workspace does not automatically make every crate visible to every other crate. Nor does it guarantee there is only one version of every external package: incompatible requirements can still resolve to multiple versions. The shared lockfile records the actual graph. Use `cargo tree` when you need to inspect it rather than assuming deduplication.

Create a workspace with two members, add a public function to the library, and call it from the CLI. Run `cargo test --workspace` to exercise all members. Then add a test that calls the library directly and compare it with a CLI-level test. The workspace boundary is a useful organizational choice when packages have separate purposes or release needs. Splitting every file into a crate would add manifest and versioning overhead without improving the design. Start with a clear library/binary split when that split reflects a real responsibility.

A workspace is also a convenient boundary for coordinated checks: formatting, linting, and tests can cover all members together while each package keeps its own public API and dependencies.
writing.feedback: The members resolve together into one `Cargo.lock`, and a shared `target` directory reuses build output. Incompatible requirements can still select two versions of a dependency.
